analysis.one_liner: Strengthens endangered species recovery rules and gives landowners tax breaks for protecting habitat.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 103 cosponsors but never got a committee vote or a floor vote in the House before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have strengthened the Endangered Species Act: habitat for listed species would have to be designated when a species is listed, recovery plans would need measurable science-based goals, permits to harm species would require performance bonds and monitoring, and citizens could sue over permit violations. To ease the burden on landowners, it offered estate tax exclusion, property tax deductions, and tax credits for landowners who sign voluntary conservation agreements. It never received a vote and died when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people would gain stronger protection for endangered wildlife and the habitats and ecosystems that support recreation, clean water, and natural heritage, with public reporting making federal wildlife decisions transparent. Landowners who protect habitat would gain tax breaks and faster permits for small projects, and tribes would gain access to cooperative conservation funding.

how_it_helps.text: Requires habitat to be designated at the time a species is listed, and requires recovery plans with measurable, science-based criteria for removing species from the endangered list.
Strengthens permits for incidental takings by requiring conservation plans consistent with recovery, performance bonds, annual monitoring reports, and permit revocation when conditions are violated.
Expands citizen lawsuits to cover violations of permits and federal wildlife opinions, and adds liability for negligently destroying endangered species habitat.

Offers landowners tax relief — estate tax exclusion, property tax deduction, and a credit for compliance costs — in exchange for voluntary conservation agreements, plus a streamlined process and a community assistance program for small landowners.

analysis.who_pays: Developers, large landowners, and industries seeking permits to harm endangered species habitat would bear new costs: stricter conservation plans, performance bonds, monitoring, and liability for damage. Taxpayers would fund roughly $175-190 million a year in federal programs, plus tax revenue lost to the new incentives.
analysis.who_pays_short: Developers and landowners seeking to build

drawbacks.text: The bill would have imposed significant new costs on developers and landowners: stricter habitat conservation plan requirements, performance bonds, monitoring, and liability for negligently damaging listed species or their habitat, which could raise housing and development costs in some areas.

Tax breaks for landowners who sign conservation agreements (estate tax exclusion, property tax deduction, compliance credit) reduce federal revenue, and the costs of the new streamlined small-permit program would be paid by the government rather than the permittee.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have strengthened species recovery and given landowners tax help and clearer permit rules, with the costs falling on developers, large landowners (through stricter permits and bonds), and federal budgets of roughly $175-190 million a year. For people who value wildlife and intact ecosystems the gains are large; the main costs are tighter constraints on land use and federal spending, which the bill tried to soften through streamlined small-permit procedures and financial incentives.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Resources and Ways and Means committees, and neither one ever voted on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Introduced March 3, 1999 by Rep. George Miller with 66 original cosponsors and referred to the Resources Committee and, for the tax provisions, to Ways and Means.
Its only further action was a request for executive comment from the Interior Department on March 9, 1999; no hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded.
Cosponsorship grew to 103 members, but no vote was ever scheduled before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Developers, large landowners, and extractive industries avoided stricter habitat rules, bonds, and liability; no one outside those interests gained.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Developers and landowners who avoided stricter rules

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 3, 1999 and built a large cosponsor list.

for.name: 103 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it substantial bipartisan-flavored support on paper.

against.name: House Resources and Ways and Means Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in its action history after referral and a request for Interior Department comment.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 95 of 103 cosponsors — with a handful of Republican and one independent cosponsor, and no recorded action ever moved it forward.

industries.industry: Real estate developers and large landowners
industries.note: The bill raises the bar for permits to harm endangered species habitat: stricter conservation plans, performance bonds, monitoring, and possible revocation. It offsets this with tax incentives and streamlined permits for small projects, but large projects face materially higher costs.

industries.industry: Extractive industries (timber, mining, oil and gas)
industries.note: Stronger habitat protection, citizen suits, and damage liability constrain activity on land these industries use; their costs rise where endangered species are present.
Federal funding rises to roughly $175-190 million a year, with new roles for independent scientists, monitoring, and habitat restoration work.
